name: Polyunsaturated fatty acid supplements
short: Omega-3 supplements were linked to more atrial fibrillation in heart trials (25% higher risk, more above 1 g/day); trial reviews differ on bleeding, with more risk at high doses of purified EPA.
text: Most of the cited evidence concerns marine omega-3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA). In a meta-analysis of 7 cardiovascular outcome trials in 81,210 people followed for about 4.9 years, omega-3 supplements were associated with a 25% higher risk of atrial fibrillation, with a greater risk in trials testing more than 1 g a day. A meta-analysis of 90 randomised trials found higher odds of diarrhoea, altered taste and bleeding tendency (odds ratio 1.26) with omega-3 than with placebo, and lower rates of back pain, with no report of definite omega-3-related serious adverse events. A separate meta-analysis of 11 randomised trials in 120,643 patients found no overall difference in bleeding, haemorrhagic stroke, intracranial or gastrointestinal bleeding, but high-dose purified EPA was linked to a 50% higher relative risk of bleeding (a 0.6% absolute increase); bleeding risk was related to EPA dose but not to background antiplatelet treatment. For omega-6 fats, a Cochrane review of 19 randomised trials in 6461 people (7 of supplemental gamma-linolenic acid and 12 of linoleic acid; the omega-6 fats usually replaced saturated or monounsaturated fats in the diet) followed for one to eight years found low-quality evidence of little or no difference in all-cause mortality or cardiovascular events; the abstract does not describe other adverse events.
